analysis.one_liner: Waives FDA device registration fees for small U.S. manufacturers and charges foreign-owned companies eight times the fee.
analysis.headline: Introduced with zero cosponsors, the bill has sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee without a hearing or vote since July 20, 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the small-business waiver for the Food and Drug Administration's annual medical-device establishment registration fee. U.S. companies with fewer than 20 full-time-equivalent employees, including affiliates, would automatically get the fee waived entirely for three years and half-waived for two more, and FDA could not deny a waiver because the company skipped the fee in earlier years. Foreign-owned companies would be barred from the waiver and would pay eight times the normal registration fee.
analysis.who_benefits: Small U.S. medical device manufacturers with fewer than 20 employees gain directly: they would pay nothing for the annual establishment registration fee for three years and half the fee for the next two, with no appeals process for FDA to second-guess eligibility. Domestic device firms also gain indirectly because foreign-owned competitors would pay eight times the registration fee and cannot claim the waiver, raising rivals' costs.

how_it_helps.text: Redefines a 'small business' as a device company with fewer than 20 full-time-equivalent employees including affiliates, and requires the FDA to grant those establishments a full waiver of the annual registration fee for three years, then a 50% waiver for the following two years.

Bars FDA from considering whether an establishment paid or skipped the registration fee in any earlier year, and lets establishments prove size with a recent tax return or payroll register submitted 60 days before the fee is due.
Excludes foreign-organized companies from the waiver entirely, including U.S. entities formed just to claim it.
Imposes a new registration fee on foreign-owned device establishments equal to eight times the standard domestic fee, a cost advantage for U.S.-based competitors.

analysis.who_pays: The FDA's medical device user-fee revenue shrinks wherever small firms' registration fees are waived, which under the device user-fee program means less money for the device review program unless offset elsewhere. Foreign-owned device establishments pay eight times the registration fee, a cost likely to flow into device prices. Small firms also take on new paperwork: a tax return or payroll register filed 60 days before the fee deadline, and after the five-year waiver window expires they owe the full fee again.
analysis.who_pays_short: FDA fee revenue; foreign-owned device makers

drawbacks.text: Every fee waived comes out of the FDA device user-fee pool that funds device review and registration oversight; the 100%-for-three-years, 50%-for-two-years structure is a direct revenue loss, only partly offset by the new 8x fee on foreign companies.

FDA may not consider an applicant's past payment history, so an establishment that simply never paid the fee in prior years can still qualify, and the bill replaces the waiver request process with a 'non-reviewability' provision, meaning denied applicants appear to have no appeal.
The eightfold fee on foreign-owned establishments would likely be passed through to U.S. hospitals and patients in the price of imported devices.

The relief is temporary: eligibility expires after the five-year coverage period, after which small firms owe the full fee again, creating a cost cliff for businesses that sized themselves around the waiver.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the small device startups the bill targets, three years of a waived annual registration fee is real but modest money. The offsetting costs are diffuse: less FDA user-fee revenue for device oversight, potentially higher prices on imported devices from the 8x foreign fee, and a hard expiration that returns small firms to the full fee after five years. The anti-gaming provisions (tax-return proof, foreign exclusion, SBA size standards) are sensible, but the ban on considering payment history and the removal of any review process are poorly designed. On balance this is a narrow industry-relief bill, not a measure with large public benefits.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2026 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has sat for weeks with no hearing, no markup, and no vote, and with only a few months left in the session it will likely die there quietly.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott Perry introduced the bill on July 20, 2026, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which holds jurisdiction over FDA law.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor scheduling — appears in the action history after the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has moved: the current FDA fee rules remain in effect, so small device makers keep paying the registration fee and foreign-owned establishments avoid the eightfold fee. The bill's quiet parking in committee preserves the status quo for FDA's user-fee revenue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody yet — the status quo holds

for.name: Rep. Scott Perry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 20, 2026 and is its only sponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral for FDA legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 20, 2026; no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled since.

sides.party_line_note: Only one member of either party is attached to the bill — its Republican sponsor, with zero cosponsors — and no vote has ever occurred, so there is no partisan pattern to measure.

industries.industry: Small U.S. medical device manufacturers (under 20 employees)
industries.note: They would pay nothing for annual FDA establishment registration for three years and half the fee for two more, with FDA barred from weighing past payment history. The gain comes at the cost of FDA user-fee revenue and expires after five years.

They are excluded from the waiver — even via U.S. subsidiaries formed for that purpose — and would pay eight times the standard registration fee. Because that cost would likely be passed into device prices, their loss tracks a cost to U.S. hospitals and patients too.

Waived small-business fees shrink the revenue pool that funds device registration oversight, while the 8x foreign-company fee adds some back. The program's oversight capacity is the swing item for the public.

analysis.trajectory: With the 119th Congress ending January 3, 2027 and only weeks elapsed since introduction, a single-sponsor bill with zero cosponsors and no committee action almost never reaches the floor in its first session; unless it gains cosponsors and an Energy and Commerce markup in the remaining months, it will expire when the Congress ends and would need to be reintroduced from scratch.
